newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mortgage rates rose in week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mortgage rates rose in week.

text.p: Fixed-rate mortgage rates edged higher this week after the Federal Reserve tightened credit for the first time in two years, Freddie Mac said Thursday.
Thirty-year fixed-rate mortgage rates averaged 7.97 percent this week, up slightly from 7.94 percent last week, while 15-year loan rates rose to 7.48 percent from 7.45 percent in the prior week.
One-year adjustable mortgage rates were unchanged at 5.71 percent.
Freddie Mac chief economist Robert Van Order said he expects mortgage rates to hit the 8 percent mark next week after the Federal Reserve raised short-term rates on Tuesday.
Van Order said although rates had been rising steadily over the last few weeks in anticipation of a Fed rate hike, "rates did move up a few basis points" after this week's Fed announcement.
"With this in mind, it wouldn't be surprising to see mortgage rates a little bit over 8 percent next week," Van Order said.

On Tuesday, the Fed raised short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point. It described the move -- the first since February 1995 -- as a "prudent step" designed to help prolong the economic expansion by keeping inflation low through the end of next year.

The interest-rate hike will mean higher borrowing costs for consumer and corporate loans. Many commercial banks, including Chase Manhattan, the nation's largest bank, boosted their lending rates in response to the Fed move.
A year ago, the 30-year mortgage rate averaged 7.69 percent, the 15-year 7.19 percent and the adjustable loan 5.62 percent.
Lenders charged an average of 1.8 percent in fees and points on the 30-year loan, unchanged from the previous week. Charges on 15-year loans rose to 1.8 percent from 1.7 percent.
Lenders charged 1.4 percent on adjustable loans, up from 1.3 percent last week.

Freddie Mac, which recently changed its name from Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp., is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
